title: Australia raises rates despite weakening housing as the inflation return slips into 2027
summary: On November 3 the Monetary Policy Board raised the cash rate target to 4.85%, a 25-basis-point increase supported by six members. Three preferred to leave it at 4.60%. The decision followed a sharp upward revision to staff inflation forecasts. The Board believed inflation could remain above 3% for the coming year, reaching the upper end of the 2–3% target range around three quarters later than previously expected. It saw a growing risk that a prolonged period of high inflation would affect expectations. At the same time, the housing market was weakening and unemployment was rising. The statement records the minority vote without assigning members specific reasons (November decision).

The September-quarter readings showed the distinction between imported costs and domestic persistence. Headline CPI rose 3.9% over the year, and trimmed mean inflation reached 3.7%. Fuel prices had increased substantially, but market services also registered sizeable increases and firms across industries described sustained cost pressure. Strong AI-related investment was raising prices for technology-related goods. Domestic capacity was judged tighter than staff had estimated earlier. The Board reported that some measures of inflation expectations had risen. The quarterly outlook also reported that longer-term expectations derived from financial markets remained consistent with central bank targets. The concern was therefore the risk and breadth of persistence, rather than evidence of a uniform shift at every horizon (decision and November Statement on Monetary Policy, overview).

The change from August was largest over the coming year. Staff’s year-ended CPI forecasts for December 2026 and June 2027 each rose 0.9 percentage points, to 4.5% and 3.7%. Trimmed mean inflation for June 2027 rose half a point to 3.5%. By December 2027 headline and trimmed mean inflation were projected at 2.7% and 2.9%, respectively. Both were forecast at 2.5% in June 2028. Those numbers describe a return inside the band before convergence to its midpoint. They also preserve the distinction between the temporary impact of fuel and broader price pressures. Rising input costs, stronger prior domestic capacity pressure and a higher market-implied policy rate all entered the new forecast together (November outlook, overview forecast table).

The costs of tighter financial conditions were becoming more visible. September house prices were nearly 5% below their March peak. Higher rates and tax changes announced in the federal budget both contributed to the housing downturn in staff’s account. The unemployment rate averaged 4.6% in the September quarter, exceeding expectations. Increased labour force participation amid cost-of-living pressures accounted for much of the surprise, while employment growth held up. Staff expected unemployment to average 5.1% in the December 2028 quarter, up from 4.8% in August. Further slowing in consumption and dwelling investment was partly offset by business investment, particularly in data centres. An account portraying unemployment as rising solely because jobs were already disappearing would misread the incoming evidence (November outlook, domestic activity and forecast table).

Financial conditions also varied by borrower. Staff judged policy restrictive and assessed that the cash rate stood slightly above the upper end of its range of central neutral-rate estimates. New housing lending had fallen sharply, yet business credit was growing strongly and corporate risk premia were low. These facts differ from an economy-wide withdrawal of credit. The balance between household weakness and corporate investment is central to the policy trade-off. It helps explain how a majority could judge another increase appropriate even while GDP was projected to grow below trend and spare capacity was expected to emerge in 2027 (November outlook, financing conditions and activity outlook).

Ahead of the meeting, staff reported pricing consistent with roughly one and a half more increases by the middle of the following year. The forecast table used market prices as of October 28. Neither observation supplies the exact probability assigned to the November decision at 2:29 p.m. on announcement day. A market study needs that pre-release observation in addition to the six-to-three vote and the simultaneous forecast news. It should also distinguish global moves in term premia from changes in expected short rates when interpreting long Australian government yields (decision, vote, and November outlook, forecast assumptions).

questions.question: How much of the forecast delay came from broader domestic inflation?
questions.detail: Break the change from the August forecast into fuel and energy components, imported technology goods and labour-intensive services. Allow for the effect of the Australian dollar and earlier energy costs reaching final prices. Test whether the distribution of service price increases widened alongside the rise in trimmed mean inflation.

questions.question: Did the housing correction have effects beyond households facing higher mortgage payments?
questions.detail: Compare turnover, spending, dwelling approvals and employment across regions with different mortgage leverage and exposure to the announced tax changes. Track renters, outright owners and recent borrowers separately where possible. Slower spending by outright owners would suggest a wealth or confidence channel in addition to direct interest expense.

questions.question: Was the rise in unemployment signalling lost demand or higher labour supply?
questions.detail: Reconstruct the September-quarter change in the unemployment rate using participation, population and employment, then examine hours, vacancies and hiring. Compare these outcomes with the November-vintage forecast rather than later revisions. A continued rise in participation with positive employment growth has different implications for slack and wage pressure from falling employment.

questions.question: Which part of the policy path repriced when the forecasts and split vote appeared?
questions.detail: Measure immediate and later meeting contracts around 2:30 p.m. Sydney time, then compare shorter forwards with long government bond yields and overseas rates. Check whether the three votes for holding offset some of the inflation forecast news. Separate the later press conference from the initial announcement.
